lessons.title: Safety and preparing to spray
lessons.html:
Why we spray paint farm equipment

Paint protects metal on trailers, implements, tanks and tractor parts from rust. It also makes equipment look good and keeps safety markings visible. In the workshop you may spray primer and top coat on repaired parts, new fabrications or whole implements.

Dangers of spray painting

  • Fumes and mist: paint, thinners and hardeners give off vapours that can harm your lungs, brain and liver. Some hardeners (isocyanates) can cause serious breathing problems.
  • Fire and explosion: thinners and paint mist burn easily.
  • Skin and eyes: paint and solvents irritate and can be absorbed through skin.
  • Compressed air: high pressure air can injure you. Never point a spray gun or air line at anyone.

Personal protective equipment

  • A respirator that is right for the paint you use. Read the paint label and safety data sheet to see what is needed. A simple dust mask is not enough for solvent paints.
  • Safety glasses or goggles
  • Chemical-resistant gloves
  • Overalls that cover arms and legs

The work area

  • Spray in a spray booth or a well-ventilated area away from other workers.
  • No smoking, open flames, grinding or welding nearby.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher close.
  • Keep only the paint you need for the job in the area. Close tins when not in use.
  • Protect the floor and nearby machines with masking paper or plastic.

Read the label

The paint label and technical data sheet tell you the mixing ratio, which thinner to use, how long the mixed paint lasts (pot life), drying times and the PPE needed. Always follow them. Do not guess mixing ratios.

lessons.title: Surface preparation
lessons.html:
Good paint starts with good preparation

Most paint failures, like peeling and blistering, happen because the surface was not prepared well. Preparation takes longer than spraying, but it is the most important part.

Steps to prepare a metal surface

  1. Clean: wash off mud, grease and oil. Use a degreaser and water, then let it dry.
  2. Remove rust and loose paint: use a wire brush, grinder with wire wheel, flap disc or sandpaper. Wear eye protection and gloves. For badly rusted parts, sandblasting may be used by a trained person.
  3. Sand: sand old paint that is still sound, so the new paint can grip. Feather the edges where old paint meets bare metal.
  4. Fill: fill small dents with body filler if needed, let it harden, and sand smooth.
  5. Wipe down: use a clean cloth with the recommended wax and grease remover to remove dust and fingerprints.
  6. Mask: cover parts that must not get paint, like hoses, decals, bearings, grease nipples, lights and number plates. Use masking tape and paper.

Primer

Primer is the first coat on bare metal. It protects against rust and helps the top coat stick. Use the primer recommended for the top coat. Some primers need light sanding before the top coat.

Handling the prepared part

After cleaning, do not touch the surface with bare hands. Skin oils can stop paint from sticking. Wear clean gloves.

Safety while preparing

Grinding and sanding make dust and sparks. Keep sparks away from paint and thinners. Wear a dust mask, eye protection and hearing protection when using power tools.

lessons.title: Spraying, cleaning up and checking the finish
lessons.html:
Using the spray gun

Setting up

  • Mix the paint exactly as the label says, using a mixing cup with ratio marks. Stir well.
  • Strain the paint through a paint strainer into the gun cup to remove lumps.
  • Set the air pressure as recommended by the gun maker and the paint data sheet.
  • Adjust the fan size and paint flow. Test on a piece of scrap metal or cardboard first.

Spraying technique

  1. Hold the gun at a right angle to the surface, at the distance recommended for the gun, usually about a hand span.
  2. Move your whole arm, not just the wrist, so the distance stays the same.
  3. Start moving before you pull the trigger and release the trigger before you stop.
  4. Overlap each pass by about half.
  5. Move at a steady speed. Too slow causes runs; too fast gives a thin, dry coat.
  6. Do edges and corners first, then flat areas.
  7. Allow the flash-off time on the label between coats.

Common faults

FaultLikely cause
Runs and sagsToo much paint, gun too close or moving too slowly
Orange peel (rough texture)Wrong pressure, paint too thick or gun too far
Fish eyes (small craters)Oil or silicone on the surface
Dry sprayGun too far or moving too fast

Cleaning up

  • Clean the gun straight after use with the correct thinner or gun wash, following the maker's instructions.
  • Never spray thinners into the open air to clean the gun; use a gun cleaning station or container.
  • Put used rags in a closed metal bin. Oily, solvent rags can catch fire.
  • Dispose of waste paint and thinners as hazardous waste. Never pour them down drains or onto the ground.

Key points

  • Wear the respirator, gloves and eye protection the label requires.
  • No flames, sparks or smoking near spraying.
  • Clean, de-rust, sand, degrease and mask before painting.
  • Mix paint exactly as the label says and test the spray pattern.
  • Keep the gun at a constant distance and overlap passes by half.
  • Clean the gun after use and dispose of waste safely.
